Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold, let $\bar g$
be a smooth background metric with Levi-Civita connection $\bar\nabla$, and let
$H^a=g^{bc}(\Gamma^a{}_{bc}-\bar\Gamma^a{}_{bc})$ be the harmonic-gauge vector
of [[def-gr-harmonic-gauge-and-reduced-equations]]. Then:

**(a) [principal part]** Let $\hat g$ be a smooth Lorentzian metric on an open
set $U\subseteq M$ and let $h$ be a smooth symmetric covariant $2$-tensor on
$U$. The derivative at $\hat g$ in the direction $h$ of the operator
$g\mapsto\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}[g]-\bar\nabla_{(a}H_{b)}[g]$ equals
$$-\tfrac12\hat g^{cd}\,\bar\nabla_c\bar\nabla_d h_{ab}+L_{ab}(h,\bar\nabla h;\hat g,\bar g),$$
where $L$ is a smooth expression linear in $h$ and its first
$\bar\nabla$-derivatives with coefficients built from $\hat g,\hat g^{-1}$, its first and second
$\bar\nabla$-derivatives, $\bar g$ and the background curvature. Thus the
coefficients depend on the full second jet of the linearization metric. In particular the principal symbol is
$-\tfrac12\hat g^{cd}\xi_c\xi_d$ times the identity on the metric slot at every
covector $\xi$.

**(b) [first-order reduction]** Fix constants $\kappa>0$, $\Lambda\in\mathbb R$ and a prescribed smooth symmetric covariant $2$-tensor field $T$ on the chart domain. Fix a chart $(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3)$ with
$x^0=t$. Introduce the metric variables
$$u:=\bigl(g_{ab},\ p_{ab}:=\bar\nabla_0g_{ab},\ q_{abi}:=\bar\nabla_ig_{ab}\bigr)$$
(symmetry in $a,b$ understood) and the relation variables $\bar\nabla_0g_{ab}-p_{ab}=0$ and $\bar\nabla_0q_{abi}-\bar\nabla_ip_{ab}=\mathcal C_{abi}$, where $\mathcal C_{abi}=-\bar R^c{}_{a0i}g_{cb}-\bar R^c{}_{b0i}g_{ac}$. Second covariant derivatives include their derivative-slot connection. These known background-curvature terms are zeroth order in the first-order state and vanish for the flat coordinate background. Then the reduced Einstein equation can be solved for the second time derivatives in the form
$$\bar\nabla_0p_{ab}=-(g^{00})^{-1}\Bigl[2g^{0i}\bar\nabla_ip_{ab}+g^{ij}\bar\nabla_iq_{abj}+R_{ab}(x,u,T;\kappa,\Lambda,\bar g)\Bigr],$$
where the source is smooth in the first-order metric state and the prescribed matter data, with no derivatives of $T$, and includes $2\kappa(T_{ab}-\tfrac12(g^{cd}T_{cd})g_{ab})+2\Lambda g_{ab}$. The resulting first-order system for $u$ is symmetric hyperbolic on every
region where $g^{00}<0$ and the spatial block $(g^{ij})$ is positive definite:
the coefficient of $\bar\nabla_0u$ is the block diagonal
$\operatorname{diag}(I,-g^{00}I,g^{ij}I)$ (on the three slots
$g,p,q$), which is positive definite there, and the coefficients of the spatial
derivatives are symmetric. More generally, in a coupled reduction one may substitute a specified smooth algebraic stress map $T_{ab}=\mathcal T_{ab}(x,u,z)$, symmetric in $a,b$, where $z$ is a specified additional first-order matter state ranging in an open Euclidean set. This keeps the same metric principal matrices; symmetric hyperbolicity of the combined metric-matter system requires a separate check of the matter equations.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $s\ge5$ be an integer, let $O\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, let $I$ be an open time interval, let $I_0\subseteq I$ be a compact interval, and let $F:I\times\mathbb T^3\times O\to\mathbb R^{m'}$ and $A:I\times\mathbb T^3\times O\to M_{m'}(\mathbb R)$ be smooth. Fix compact $K\subseteq O$ and $R\ge0$. Constants below depend on these data and are uniform in $t\in I_0$. For $u,v\in H^s$ with values in $K$ and norms at most $R$:

**(a)** $\|F(t,\cdot,u)\|_{H^j}\le C(1+\|u\|_{H^s})$ for $0\le j\le s$.

**(b)** $\|F(t,\cdot,u)-F(t,\cdot,v)\|_{H^{s-1}}\le C\|u-v\|_{H^{s-1}}$. The same bound holds at order zero.

**(c)** For $1\le j=|\alpha|\le s-1$, $\|[D^\alpha,A(t,\cdot,u)]w\|_2\le C\|w\|_{H^{j-1}}$. For $|\alpha|=s$, $\|[D^\alpha,A(t,\cdot,u)]w\|_2\le C\|w\|_{H^{s-1}}$. Commutators are interpreted distributionally by their Leibniz expansion, even if the two individual order-$j$ terms are not separately in $L^2$.

**(d)** For $0\le j\le s-1$, $\|A(t,\cdot,u)w\|_{H^j}\le C\|w\|_{H^j}$.

**(e)** Let $n\ge6$ be an integer, $\rho\ge0$ and $z\in H^n$ with values in $K$ and $\|z\|_{H^{n-1}}\le\rho$. Then $\|F(t,\cdot,z)\|_{H^n}\le C_\rho(1+\|z\|_{H^n})$. Moreover for $w\in H^{n-1}$ and $|\alpha|\le n$,
$$\|[D^\alpha,A(t,\cdot,z)]w\|_2\le C_\rho\bigl(\|w\|_{H^{n-1}}+(1+\|z\|_{H^n})\|w\|_{H^{n-2}}\bigr).$$
The same estimates apply to any smooth coefficient obtained from $F,A$ by differentiation or by a smooth matrix inverse where that inverse exists on a neighborhood of $I_0\times\mathbb T^3\times K$.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold, and let $\Sigma\subseteq M$ be a smooth spacelike embedded hypersurface with future unit normal $n$, induced Riemannian metric $h$ and second fundamental form $K(X,Y)=g(\nabla_Xn,Y)$ ([[def-gr-spacelike-hypersurfaces-and-cauchy-sets]], [[lem-gr-spacelike-hypersurface-normal-and-second-fundamental-form]]). Write $D$ for the Levi-Civita connection of $h$, $R^h$ for its curvature operator in the same operator convention as the ambient curvature, and $S_h$ for its scalar curvature. Explicitly distinguish the lowered tensor from the operator pairing by setting
$$\mathcal R^g(A,B,C,D):=g(R^g(C,D)B,A),\qquad \mathcal R^h(A,B,C,D):=h(R^h(C,D)B,A).$$
Thus $\mathcal R^g_{abcd}=R_{abcd}$ in [[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]]; in particular $g(R^g(X,Y)Z,W)=\mathcal R^g(W,Z,X,Y)$. Let $G$ be the Einstein tensor defined there. At every $p\in\Sigma$ and for all $X,Y,Z,W\in T_p\Sigma$:

**(a) Gauss equation.**
$$\mathcal R^g(X,Y,Z,W)=\mathcal R^h(X,Y,Z,W)+K(X,Z)K(Y,W)-K(X,W)K(Y,Z).$$
Equivalently, in operator order,
$$g(R^g(X,Y)Z,W)=h(R^h(X,Y)Z,W)+K(Y,Z)K(X,W)-K(X,Z)K(Y,W).$$

**(b) Codazzi equation.**
$$g(R^g(X,Y)Z,n)=(D_YK)(X,Z)-(D_XK)(Y,Z).$$

**(c) Normal projections.** Define $(\operatorname{div}_hK)(Y)=h^{ij}(D_{e_i}K)(e_j,Y)$, $\tau=\operatorname{tr}_hK=h^{ij}K_{ij}$ and $|K|_h^2=h^{ik}h^{jl}K_{ij}K_{kl}$. Then
$$G(n,n)=\tfrac12(S_h+\tau^2-|K|_h^2),\qquad G(n,Y)=(\operatorname{div}_hK)(Y)-D_Y\tau.$$

**(d) Constraint equations.** If the tensor equation $G+\Lambda g=\kappa T$ holds at $p$, for a smooth symmetric covariant $2$-tensor $T$ and real constants $\kappa,\Lambda$, then
$$S_h+\tau^2-|K|_h^2=2\Lambda+2\kappa T(n,n),\qquad (\operatorname{div}_hK)(Y)-D_Y\tau=\kappa T(n,Y).$$
With $\rho=T(n,n)$ and $j(Y)=-T(n,Y)$, the second equation is $(\operatorname{div}_hK)(Y)-D_Y\tau=-\kappa j(Y)$.

Let $(M,g,N,o)$ be an oriented, time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$, with its metric-selected Levi–Civita connection and independent orientation as in [[def-emg-lorentzian-forms]]. Use length coordinates $x^0=ct$ and the curvature and Hodge conventions of [[def-emg-electrovacuum-cauchy-system]] and [[lem-emg-lorentz-hodge-calculus]]. Fix $c>0$, $G_N>0$, $\mu_0>0$, $\Lambda\in\mathbb R$, and put $\kappa=8\pi G_N/c^4$.

The **trivial-potential sector** consists of a global smooth real one-form $A\in\Omega^1(M)$ and a global smooth complex scalar field $\varphi\in C^\infty(M;\mathbb C)$. It defines the exact real two-form $F:=dA$ and the charged derivative

$$\pi_a:=(D\varphi)_a:=\nabla_a\varphi-i\lambda A_a\varphi=\partial_a\varphi-i\lambda A_a\varphi,$$

where $\lambda\in\mathbb R$ is an arbitrary fixed coupling. Define $D_a\pi_b:=\nabla_a\pi_b-i\lambda A_a\pi_b$, with the conjugate derivative using $+i\lambda A_a$, and $D_a\pi^a:=g^{ab}D_a\pi_b$. Let $\mathcal U\subset\mathbb R$ be open with $|\varphi|^2(M)\subset\mathcal U$, let $V\in C^\infty(\mathcal U;\mathbb R)$, and fix $K_\varphi>0$. Define

$$L_\varphi:=g^{ab}\overline{\pi_a}\pi_b+V(|\varphi|^2),\qquad S_\varphi:=-\frac{K_\varphi}{2c}\int_M L_\varphi\,\mathrm{vol}_g,$$

where on a noncompact $M$ the integral is used when finite and otherwise only compactly supported action differences are used. The scalar equation, current vector, and scalar stress tensor are

$$D_a\pi^a-V'(|\varphi|^2)\varphi=0,\qquad j^a:=K_\varphi\lambda\operatorname{Im}(\overline\varphi\pi^a),$$

$$T^\varphi_{ab}:=K_\varphi\operatorname{Re}(\overline{\pi_a}\pi_b)-\frac{K_\varphi}{2}g_{ab}L_\varphi.$$

Put

$$T^{\mathrm{EM}}_{ab}:=\frac{1}{\mu_0}\left(F_{ac}F_b{}^c-\frac14g_{ab}F_{cd}F^{cd}\right),\qquad T_{ab}:=T^{\mathrm{EM}}_{ab}+T^\varphi_{ab}.$$

The associated **classical charged-scalar Einstein–Maxwell system** is

$$G_{ab}+\Lambda g_{ab}=\kappa T_{ab},\qquad dF=0,\qquad \nabla_aF^{ab}=-\mu_0j^b,\qquad D_a\pi^a-V'(|\varphi|^2)\varphi=0.$$

Here $G_{ab}=\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}-\tfrac12 Rg_{ab}$; all indices are raised with $g^{-1}$. This is a definition of a mathematical system, not an adopted physical postulate or a claim about nature. It is restricted to a trivial real-potential sector: $F$ is exact, no nontrivial $U(1)$ bundle is included, and $\lambda$ is not quantized. The scalar is classical, and neither $K_\varphi$ nor $\lambda$ is tied to a Planck constant.

For formal SI bookkeeping in length coordinates, assign $[g_{ab}]=1$, $[x^a]=\mathrm m$, $[c]=\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $[G_N]=\mathrm{m^3\,kg^{-1}\,s^{-2}}$, $[\mu_0]=\mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}$, $[\Lambda]=\mathrm{m^{-2}}$, $[A_a]=\mathrm{Wb\,m^{-1}}$, $[F_{ab}]=\mathrm{Wb\,m^{-2}}$, $[\varphi]=1$, $[\lambda]=\mathrm{Wb^{-1}}$, $[\pi_a]=\mathrm{m^{-1}}$, $[V]=\mathrm{m^{-2}}$, and $[K_\varphi]=\mathrm{J\,m^{-1}}$. These give $[j^a]=\mathrm{A\,m^{-2}}$, $[T_{ab}]=\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$, $[\kappa T_{ab}]=\mathrm{m^{-2}}$, and $[S_\varphi]=\mathrm{J\,s}$. They are dimensions, not measured values.

Let $M^n$ be an oriented smooth manifold without boundary. For each compact set $K\subseteq M$ there are finitely many nonnegative smooth functions $\chi_i$ with compact supports contained in connected coordinate domains $U_i$, such that $\sum_i\chi_i=1$ on a neighbourhood of $K$. For $\omega\in\Omega_c^n(M)$ define
$$\mathcal I_M(\omega)=\sum_i I_{\phi_i}(\chi_i\omega)\quad(K=\operatorname{supp}\omega),$$
using the signed chart integrals. This value is independent of the finite functions and charts. It defines a linear functional, is local under restriction to an open set containing the support, and for $n\ge1$ satisfies
$$\mathcal I_M(d\eta)=0\qquad(\eta\in\Omega_c^{n-1}(M)).$$
For $n=0$ it is the finite signed sum $\sum_{p\in\operatorname{supp}\omega}\varepsilon(p)\omega(p)$. All assertions are choice-free: no partition on the entire manifold is required.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $g:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be injective and $C^1$, with $Dg(x)$ invertible on $U$. Let $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be compactly supported Riemann integrable and suppose $\operatorname{supp}f\subseteq g(U)$. Define
$$h(x)=\begin{cases}f(g(x))|\det Dg(x)|,&x\in U,\\0,&x\notin U.\end{cases}$$
Then $h$ is compactly supported Riemann integrable and
$$\int_{\mathbb R^n}f(y)\,dy=\int_{\mathbb R^n}h(x)\,dx.$$
Every continuous real function on a closed nondegenerate rectangle $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $m\ge1$, is Riemann integrable.

Let $Q=\prod_{j<m}[a_j,b_j]$ be nondegenerate. For integrable
$f,g:Q\to\mathbb R$ and scalars $\alpha,\beta$, the function
$\alpha f+\beta g$ is integrable and its integral is
$\alpha\int_Qf+\beta\int_Qg$. If $f\le g$, then
$\int_Qf\le\int_Qg$. Also $|f|$ is integrable and
$|\int_Qf|\le\int_Q|f|$. If $a_r<c<b_r$, cutting $Q$ at the coordinate
hyperplane $x_r=c$ gives two nondegenerate subrectangles; integrability on
$Q$ is equivalent to integrability on both restrictions, and their integral
values add to the integral over $Q$.

derivations.claim: In a smooth chart, inversion of a nondegenerate $C^3$ matrix is $C^3$; the Christoffel formula therefore gives a $C^2$ connection and the curvature formula a $C^1$ tensor. Smooth coordinate changes preserve these regularities. The ordinary chain and product rules give $F,P\in C^1$, the stated continuous Euler–Lagrange expressions, and $C^1$ current and stress. Symmetry of $g^{-1}$ makes $g^{ab}\overline{P_a}P_b$ real and $\operatorname{Re}(\overline{P_a}P_b)$ symmetric; the Maxwell quadratic is also symmetric. The coordinate transformation laws follow by the chain rule, so all displayed equations compare global tensors. Commuting the continuous second partial derivatives of $A$ gives $dF=0$.

Let $K=\operatorname{supp}\omega$. Apply [F2] and multiply $\omega$ by its finitely many cutoffs. Each continuous coefficient has compact support strictly inside its chart, so zero extension is continuous and has a bounding rectangle; [F4] defines its finite integral. On a chart overlap the top-form coefficient transforms by the determinant of the smooth coordinate change. Its orientation sign converts that determinant to the absolute determinant, so [F3] gives the same signed integral in either chart. For two finite localizations $(\chi_i)$ and $(\tau_j)$, insert $\chi_i\omega=\sum_j\chi_i\tau_j\omega$ and the corresponding identity with $i,j$ exchanged. Every product has compact support in the chart intersection. Finite linearity from [F5] and the overlap identity make both sums equal to the same double sum. Thus $\mathcal I_M$ is well defined, linear and local. Empty support gives the empty sum zero.

Each action density has continuous coefficients. Configurations agreeing off a compact set have density difference supported in that set, including the curvature term, because their derivatives agree on its open complement. Step 1.2 therefore defines every stated relative action. For three mutually compactly differing configurations the density differences add on the union of their compact supports, so their relative actions add. On smooth fields the construction is precisely the same finite chart integral and the formulas in [F1]; hence it agrees with the original smooth relative action.

On the union $K$ of the three direction supports, nondegeneracy and the chosen time cone persist under a uniformly small perturbation: use finitely many chart neighborhoods of the compact set and take the minimum of their positive parameter bounds. The attained set $|\varphi|^2(K)$ is a compact subset of the open set $\mathcal U$, so uniform convergence of $|\varphi+\varepsilon\eta|^2$ keeps it inside $\mathcal U$ for small $\varepsilon$; outside $K$ nothing changes. The resulting metric is $C^3$ and the matter fields are $C^2$, with $\delta g_{ab}=-g_{ac}g_{bd}q^{cd}$. The action densities and their parameter derivatives are continuous on compact parameter-chart rectangles. Consequently these directions are actual variations of the declared class, not only formal symbols.

A real $C^3$ function $\chi$ gives $A'=A+d\chi\in C^2$ and $\varphi'=e^{i\lambda\chi}\varphi\in C^2$. The product rule gives $P'=e^{i\lambda\chi}P$ and $F'=F$, so the action density is unchanged. Pullback by a smooth orientation-preserving diffeomorphism also preserves the classical class and the density formulas. For compactly supported transformations, step 1.2 and [F3] give invariance of the relative action. These are mathematical invariances, not a physical adoption or a solution-existence theorem.

Let $M$ be a smooth Hausdorff, second-countable, oriented four-manifold without boundary. Its smooth
structure is retained throughout. A **classical finite-regularity
trivial-potential configuration** consists of a time-oriented $C^3$
Lorentzian metric $g$ of signature $(-,+,+,+)$, a global real $C^2$ one-form
$A$, and a global complex $C^2$ scalar $\varphi$. Fix
$c,G_N,\mu_0,K_\varphi>0$, $\lambda,\Lambda\in\mathbb R$, and
$V\in C^\infty(\mathcal U;\mathbb R)$ for an open
$\mathcal U\subset\mathbb R$ containing $|\varphi|^2(M)$. Set
$\kappa_E=8\pi G_N/c^4$. The curvature sign, length-coordinate convention
$x^0=ct$, and SI assignments are those of
[[def-emg-trivial-potential-charged-scalar-system]]; only these formulas and
conventions are imported, not that item's smooth-field restriction.

The Levi-Civita connection and curvature here are defined by their coordinate
formulas for this $C^3$ metric. Define

$$F_{ab}:=\partial_aA_b-\partial_bA_a,\qquad P_a:=\mathcal D_a\varphi:=\partial_a\varphi-i\lambda A_a\varphi,$$

$$\mathcal D_aP_b:=\nabla_aP_b-i\lambda A_aP_b,\qquad E_\varphi:=g^{ab}\mathcal D_aP_b-V'(|\varphi|^2)\varphi,$$

$$L_\varphi:=g^{ab}\overline{P_a}P_b+V(|\varphi|^2),\qquad j^a:=K_\varphi\lambda\operatorname{Im}(\overline\varphi P^a),$$

$$T^\varphi_{ab}:=K_\varphi\operatorname{Re}(\overline{P_a}P_b)-\frac{K_\varphi}{2}g_{ab}L_\varphi,\qquad T^{\mathrm{EM}}_{ab}:=\mu_0^{-1}\left(F_{ac}F_b{}^c-\frac14g_{ab}F_{cd}F^{cd}\right).$$

Conjugate charged derivatives use the opposite gauge sign. All indices are
raised with $g^{-1}$. Thus $F,P$ are $C^1$, $j,T^\varphi,T^{\mathrm{EM}}$
are $C^1$, $E_\varphi$ and $\nabla_aF^{ab}$ are continuous, and the
Einstein tensor $G$ is $C^1$. The **classical charged-scalar equations** are
the pointwise equations

$$dF=0,\qquad \nabla_aF^{ab}=-\mu_0j^b,\qquad E_\varphi=0,\qquad G_{ab}+\Lambda g_{ab}=\kappa_E(T^{\mathrm{EM}}_{ab}+T^\varphi_{ab}).$$

Here $dF=0$ already follows from $F=dA$ with $A\in C^2$. These are equations
for the declared classical fields; they do not assert existence, smoothness
improvement, or a weaker distributional theory.

For a continuous compactly supported real top form $\omega$, define
$\mathcal I_M(\omega)$ by a finite smooth cutoff localization near its
support and the signed Riemann integrals of the resulting chart
coefficients, extended by zero. The construction and its independence are
proved below. For a complex top form extend $\mathcal I_M$ by integrating
its real and imaginary parts separately. For a configuration
$X=(g,A,\varphi)$ put

$$\mathscr L(X):=\left[\frac{c^3}{16\pi G_N}(R(g)-2\Lambda)-\frac{1}{4\mu_0c}F_{ab}F^{ab}-\frac{K_\varphi}{2c}L_\varphi\right]\mathrm{vol}_g.$$

If $X_1=X_0$ outside a compact set, its **relative total action** is
$S(X_1;X_0):=\mathcal I_M(\mathscr L(X_1)-\mathscr L(X_0))$. The scalar
and Maxwell relative actions are defined by their respective summands. No
subtraction of divergent global integrals is intended. When the separate
global integrals are defined and finite, this agrees with their difference.

Allowed independent directions are smooth compactly supported symmetric
inverse-metric tensors $q^{ab}$, real one-forms $\alpha$, and complex scalars
$\eta$. Near zero parameter use

$$g_\varepsilon^{-1}=g^{-1}+\varepsilon q,\qquad A_\varepsilon=A+\varepsilon\alpha,\qquad\varphi_\varepsilon=\varphi+\varepsilon\eta.$$

The parameter interval is restricted to preserve signature, time orientation,
and the potential domain. Stationarity means that the derivative of the
relative total action vanishes for every such direction. These definitions
include the original smooth trivial-potential system as a subclass, with its
same action coefficients and tensors. They do not change the separate
nontrivial-circle-bundle formulation or impose an integer condition on the
real coupling $\lambda$.

For $n=0$ it is the finite signed sum $\sum_{p\in\operatorname{supp}\omega}\varepsilon(p)\omega(p)$. All assertions are choice-free: no partition on the entire manifold is required.
Every continuous real function on a closed nondegenerate rectangle $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $m\ge1$, is Riemann integrable.

Let $A\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ and $B\subseteq\mathbb R^q$ be nondegenerate closed rectangles, and let $f:A\times B\to\mathbb R$ be Riemann integrable. Then the four lower and upper section-integral functions of [[def-sections-and-iterated-riemann-integrals]] are Riemann integrable and
$$\int_A\ell_B=\int_Au_B=\int_{A\times B}f=\int_B\ell_A=\int_Bu_A.$$

If the $B$-sections are integrable outside a content-zero set $N\subseteq A$, every bounded exceptionally completed function $h$ with $h(x)=\int_Bf_x$ for $x\notin N$ is integrable and
$$\int_{A\times B}f=\int_Ah.$$
The same assertion holds with the coordinate blocks exchanged. In particular, when every section in an order is integrable, the ordinary iterated integral in that order exists and equals the multiple integral. The theorem does not assert that every section of an integrable function is integrable.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Let $Q=\prod_{j<m}[a_j,b_j]$ be nondegenerate. For integrable
$f,g:Q\to\mathbb R$ and scalars $\alpha,\beta$, the function
$\alpha f+\beta g$ is integrable and its integral is
$\alpha\int_Qf+\beta\int_Qg$. If $f\le g$, then
$\int_Qf\le\int_Qg$. Also $|f|$ is integrable and

derivations.claim: Fix the compact support $K$ of the directions. Use [F2]'s finite smooth localization near $K$, independently of the variation parameter. In each chart the localized density difference and its parameter derivative are continuous on a fixed compact parameter-rectangle product: every density is a smooth algebraic expression in the nondegenerate metric, its derivatives through order two, and the matter fields through order one. The families in [F1] have the required joint derivatives. The one-variable fundamental theorem gives the difference quotient as the average of those parameter derivatives along the parameter segment. Uniform continuity on this compact product makes that quotient converge uniformly to the derivative at zero. Monotonicity and the absolute-value estimate [F6], compared with the constant $\sup_Q|f|$, give $|\int_Q f|\le\operatorname{vol}(Q)\sup_Q|f|$; this passes the limit through each finite Riemann integral. Thus the relative actions can be differentiated by differentiating their densities, even when the background global actions diverge.

Let $W$ be any compactly supported $C^1$ vector field. Write $w=\sqrt{|\det g|}$. The Christoffel formula and determinant derivative give $\Gamma^a{}_{ab}=\partial_b\log w$, hence $\nabla_aW^a\mathrm{vol}_g=\partial_a(wW^a)d^4x$ in a positive chart. For each finite cutoff $\chi_i$ in [F2], $w\chi_iW^a$ extends by zero to a $C^1$ compactly supported coefficient on a bounding rectangle. Its partial derivatives and all sections are continuous, so [F3]–[F5] integrate its coordinate divergence to zero: the opposite-face values vanish. Summing over $i$ gives the same result for $W$, because $\sum_i\chi_i=1$ and $\sum_i d\chi_i=0$ near its support. Therefore $\mathcal I_M((\nabla_aW^a)\mathrm{vol}_g)=0$ for this $C^1$ field. No smoothness approximation or unproved rough Stokes assertion is used.

Put $h_{ab}=\delta g_{ab}=-g_{ac}g_{bd}q^{cd}$. Differentiation of $g^{ac}g_{cb}=\delta^a_b$ and of the determinant gives $\delta w=-	frac12wg_{ab}q^{ab}$. Differentiating the coordinate formula for the Christoffel symbols and collecting the terms containing $h$ gives $$\delta\Gamma^a{}_{bc}= rac12g^{ad}(
abla_bh_{cd}+
abla_ch_{bd}-
abla_dh_{bc}).$$ To differentiate Ricci, use $R_{ab}=\partial_c\Gamma^c{}_{ab}-\partial_b\Gamma^c{}_{ac} +\Gamma^c{}_{cd}\Gamma^d{}_{ab}-\Gamma^c{}_{bd}\Gamma^d{}_{ac}$. The differentiated quadratic terms are exactly the connection terms that complete the two derivatives to $\delta R_{ab}=
abla_c\delta\Gamma^c{}_{ab}-
abla_b\delta\Gamma^c{}_{ac}$. Metric compatibility in this coordinate connection then gives $$\delta((R-2\Lambda)w)=w(G_{ab}+\Lambda g_{ab})q^{ab}+\partial_a(wV^a),\qquad V^a=g^{bc}\delta\Gamma^a{}_{bc}-g^{ab}\delta\Gamma^c{}_{bc}.$$ All expressions exist classically: $g,h$ are $C^3$, $\delta\Gamma$ is $C^2$, and $V$ is a compactly supported $C^2$ vector field. Steps 1.1–1.2 therefore yield the Einstein–Hilbert first variation $c^3(16\pi G_N)^{-1}\mathcal I_M((G+\Lambda g)_{ab}q^{ab}\mathrm{vol}_g)$.

At fixed metric, $\delta F_{ab}=\partial_a\alpha_b-\partial_b\alpha_a =2
abla_{[a}\alpha_{b]}$; torsion-freeness follows directly from symmetry of the Christoffel formula. Thus $\delta(F_{ab}F^{ab})=4F^{ab}
abla_a\alpha_b$. The $C^1$ compact vector $W^a=F^{ab}\alpha_b$ satisfies $
abla_aW^a=(
abla_aF^{ab})\alpha_b+F^{ab}
abla_a\alpha_b$. Steps 1.1–1.2 give $\delta_A S_{\mathrm{EM}}=(\mu_0c)^{-1}\mathcal I_M((
abla_aF^{ab})\alpha_b\mathrm{vol}_g)$. At fixed lower $F$, direct inverse-metric differentiation gives $\delta(F_{cd}F^{cd})=2F_{ac}F_b{}^c q^{ab}$. Combining it with $\delta w$ from step 2.1 gives $\delta_g S_{\mathrm{EM}}=-(2c)^{-1}\mathcal I_M(T^{\mathrm{EM}}_{ab}q^{ab}\mathrm{vol}_g)$. This uses only $F\in C^1$ and the declared metric class.

For $\eta=\delta\varphi$, direct differentiation gives $\delta_\varphi L_\varphi=2\operatorname{Re}(\overline{\mathcal D_a\eta}P^a+V'\overline\eta\varphi)$. The product rule is $\nabla_a(\overline\eta P^a)=\overline{\mathcal D_a\eta}P^a+\overline\eta\mathcal D_aP^a$: the opposite gauge signs cancel. Its real and imaginary parts are $C^1$ compact vector fields. Integrating their divergence by step 1.2 yields $\delta_\varphi S_\varphi=(K_\varphi/c)\operatorname{Re}\mathcal I_M(\overline\eta E_\varphi\mathrm{vol}_g)$. At fixed $g,\varphi$, $\delta_A P_a=-i\lambda\varphi\alpha_a$, so $\delta_A L_\varphi=-2\lambda\operatorname{Im}(\overline\varphi P^a)\alpha_a$, giving the claimed $j$. At fixed lower $A$ and fixed $\varphi$, $\delta_gL_\varphi=\operatorname{Re}(\overline{P_a}P_b)q^{ab}$; the volume term then gives the displayed $T^\varphi$. These calculations require no derivative beyond $\varphi\in C^2$ and $A\in C^2$.

Add steps 2.1, 3.1 and 3.2. The equality $(2c)^{-1}=[c^3/(16\pi G_N)]\kappa_E$ gives exactly the total first variation in the Statement, with its three independent directions. Its coefficients are continuous; the metric coefficient is symmetric. To see that testing detects a nonzero continuous component, take a positive chart where that component has one strict sign. A nonnegative smooth bump supported inside that chart, positive on a smaller closed rectangle, has a strictly positive signed pairing with the component times $w>0$. Such a bump can be taken as $e^{-1/(r^2-|x|^2)}$ inside a coordinate ball and zero outside. The resulting integral is nonzero: on the smaller rectangle the continuous sign-adjusted coefficient has a positive lower bound $a>0$, so its integral is at least $a$ times that rectangle volume by [F6]. Cutting a containing rectangle along the smaller rectangle faces and using coordinate-slice additivity in [F6] shows the full integral is at least that positive value, since the integrand is nonnegative on the remainder. A one-form test isolates any connection component; diagonal and symmetrized off-diagonal metric tests isolate every symmetric component. Scalar tests $\eta=f$ and $\eta=if$ isolate the real and imaginary parts of $E_\varphi$. Therefore stationarity for all these tests forces all three coefficients to vanish pointwise. Conversely their pointwise vanishing makes every first variation zero. The identity $dF=0$ in [F1] supplies the remaining homogeneous equation.

The charged product rule gives $\nabla_a j^a=K_\varphi\lambda\operatorname{Im}(\overline{P_a}P^a+\overline\varphi\mathcal D_aP^a)$. The first contraction is real and $V'$ is real, giving the stated current identity. Differentiating $T^\varphi$ and using $\partial_b L_\varphi=2\operatorname{Re}(\overline{P^a}\mathcal D_bP_a)+2V'\operatorname{Re}(\overline\varphi P_b)$ gives $$\nabla_a(T^\varphi)^a{}_b=K_\varphi\operatorname{Re}\left(\overline{E_\varphi}P_b+\overline{P^a}(\mathcal D_aP_b-\mathcal D_bP_a)\right).$$ The symmetric Christoffel terms cancel in the difference. Expanding $P=\partial\varphi-i\lambda A\varphi$ and commuting the continuous second scalar partial derivatives gives $\mathcal D_aP_b-\mathcal D_bP_a=-i\lambda F_{ab}\varphi$. Its contribution to the real part is $-K_\varphi\lambda F_{ab}\operatorname{Im}(\overline\varphi P^a)=F_{ba}j^a$. This proves the two scalar off-shell identities using only first derivatives of $P$ and $C^2$ scalar partials.
